ABSTRACT
Efficient generation of substitution boxes (S-boxes) with strong cryptographic properties is essential for securing modern digital
systems, particularly in resource-constrained environments such as the Internet of Things (IoT) and cloud computing. However,
constructing dynamic S-boxes often incurs significant computational overhead, which can affect encryption performance. We
propose an efficient S-box generation algorithm that combines elliptic curve point generation with a mutation-based optimization.
Our approach constructs cryptographically robust 𝑛× 𝑛S-boxes in three stages: (1) generating points on an elliptic curve over a
finite field, (2) generating an initial S-box from these points, and (3) applying a mutation operation to improve nonlinearity and
other cryptographic properties. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that the proposed method generates a secure 8 × 8 S-box
on an average of 0.0009 s and produces 10,000 randomized S-boxes in 1.2169 s. Comparative analysis indicates that our generator
operates at a speed of at least eight times faster than existing state-of-the-art generators, without compromising security against
standard cryptanalytic attacks. We further validate the practical utility of our generator in the context of image encryption. The
results show that the method effectively secures the image data, even when the original image exhibits high inter-pixel correlation,
highlighting its applicability to real-world cryptographic systems.

Introduction
In modern cryptography and secure communication, the substi-
tution box (S-box) functions as an essential component in vari-
ous cryptographic algorithms. S-boxes hold an important role in
data encryption and decryption, making a significant contribu-
tion to the overall security of information in numerous digital
applications. For an integer 𝑛, an 𝑛× 𝑛bijective S-box establishes
a one-to-one correspondence, ensuring that each set of 𝑛input
bits is uniquely mapped to a corresponding set of 𝑛output bits,
and vice versa. The main objective of an S-box is to introduce

method that uses a linear combination of Logistic and Sine

developed a robust algorithm for S-box generation by using a
two-dimensional (2D) enhanced quadratic map, effectively elim-
inating fixed points, reverse fixed points, and short cycles to pro-
duce strong keyed S-boxes. Al Khayyat et al. [5] developed a
method for constructing robust S-boxes by combining a 4D hyper-
chaotic system with an enhanced Josephus permutation. Luo
et al. [6] proposed a method for constructing S-boxes based on
the Arnold chaotic map. Their approach integrates chaos the-
ory with algebraic modeling to generate robust S-boxes. Although
S-box generators using chaotic maps have revealed promising
results for producing secure S-boxes, the reliability of chaotic
maps in terms of sensitivity and randomness is questionable in
practical applications due to precision limitations [7]. In addi-
tion, cryptographers have increasingly used optimization tech-
niques to enhance the cryptographic strength of substitution
boxes (S-boxes). For example, the method proposed in [8] uti-
lizes sine-cosine optimization to generate robust S-box structures.
Similarly, Lawah et al. [9] introduced a design based on the Grey
Wolf Optimizer combined with a chaotic map to improve non-
linearity. In [10], a heuristic algorithm initialized using chaotic
opposition-based learning is used to construct S-boxes with opti-
mal security characteristics. Furthermore, a hybrid technique
presented in [11] combines Harris Hawks Optimization with the
Booster algorithm to efficiently produce highly nonlinear S-boxes
while reducing computational overhead.
In recent years, ECs have gained significant attention in the field
of cryptography. Cryptosystems based on ECs offer enhanced
security with smaller key sizes compared to traditional crypto-
graphic systems. For example, the generators [12–20] used ECs
for the generation of S-boxes. Hayat et al. [14] introduced a novel
method to produce 8 × 8 S-boxes using ECs over a prime field.
Similarly, Hayat and Azam [15] proposed a novel method for pro-
ducing S-boxes and generating pseudo-random numbers using a
total order on an EC over a prime field. These algorithms [14, 15]
primarily rely on the 𝑥-coordinates of points on the EC. However,
they exhibit a time complexity of (𝑝), where 𝑝is the underlying
prime. Furthermore, the outcomes of these algorithms are uncer-
tain, as they may or may not produce an S-box for a given set
of input parameters, independent of the underlying EC. In con-
trast, Azam et al. [16] used specific orderings on a special class of
ECs known as Mordell elliptic curve (MEC) over a finite field to
construct an 8 × 8 S-box in a constant time. Each of these meth-
ods [14–16] can produce only one S-box for a specific EC. How-
ever, an effective S-box generator should efficiently produce mul-
tiple secure S-boxes that are uncorrelated. Azam et al. [17] pro-
posed an innovative approach for generating S-boxes with MECs,
ensuring that each valid input results in a corresponding S-box.
This method achieves a space complexity of (𝑛) for an S-box
of size 𝑛and a prime 𝑝of the MEC, with a time complexity of
(𝑛𝑝). Ibrahim et al. [18] constructed an S-box generator by gen-
erating points on ECs to create a permutation code, which is sub-
sequently used to produce S-boxes. Murtaza et al. [19] presented
an efficient S-box generation algorithm for lightweight cryptog-
raphy using ECs. Alali et al. [20] used EC cryptography within
the binary Galois field extension to construct effective S-boxes for
enhanced image encryption security. Khan et al. [21] designed a
novel method for generating dynamic and secure S-boxes using
elliptic curves. Haider et al. [22] introduced a novel method to
generate S-boxes that achieves a strong balance between crypto-
graphic robustness and computational efficiency. Recently, Mur-
taza and Hayat [12] have introduced novel algorithms for image
encryption and S-box construction using ECs. Bilal et al. [13] pro-
posed an efficient S-box construction scheme based on an EC
and applied the scheme to construct an image encryption pro-
tocol. Although EC-based generators [14–20] can produce cryp-
tographically secure S-boxes. However, the development of an
S-box generator that can generate secure S-boxes with minimal
computational overhead remains a challenging task.
The above discussion demonstrates that although existing S-box
generators based on chaotic maps and ECs demonstrate promis-
ing potential for enhancing security, several significant chal-
lenges remain unresolved. Specifically, achieving a balance
between high security and minimal computational overhead con-
tinues to be a major challenge. Chaotic maps are constrained
by precision issues that impact their practical reliability. On the
other hand, EC-based generators enhance security with smaller
key sizes but do not yet offer an efficient S-box generator that
effectively balances both security and computational efficiency.

Our Contributions
The objective of this paper is to design a novel S-box generation
algorithm capable of producing cryptographically robust S-boxes
in the least amount of computation time, making it applicable for
real-world applications. This paper presents several significant
contributions, including the following:
1. Develop an S-box generator that efficiently produces cryp-
tographically robust S-boxes in the least amount of compu-
tation time, based on supersingular elliptic curves (SSECs)
and mutation-based optimization.
2. With experimental analysis, we demonstrate that, on aver-
age, our S-box generator can produce an 8 × 8 S-box in
0.0009 s and construct 10 K randomized 8 × 8 S-boxes
in 1.2169 s. Furthermore, our method achieves speeds
that are at least eight times faster when compared with
state-of-the-art generators [3, 5, 14, 15, 17–19, 23, 24], high-
lighting its applicability for real-world applications.
3. Evaluate and compare the dynamic behavior and the
cryptographic properties of our method with existing
state-of-the-art S-box generators to determine the impor-
tance of our generator.
4. Propose a novel image encryption scheme using our S-box
generator, demonstrating its practical application.

The Proposed S-Box Generator
In this section, we explain the steps of our S-box gen-
erator, namely the elliptic curve mutation-based generator
(EC-MutGen). Our goal is to design an S-box generator based on
SSEC over a Galois field GF(2𝑚) and mutation-based optimiza-
tion to generate cryptographically strong 𝑛× 𝑛S-boxes, where 𝑚
and 𝑛are positive integers. Our newly developed S-box genera-
tion procedure consists of the following three phases. The SSEC
𝑦2 + 𝑦= 𝑥3 over 𝐺𝐹(2𝑚) has been selected due to its advanta-
geous property of having distinct y-coordinates for its points. The
construction of an S-box is significant as it necessitates 2𝑛unique
values, ranging from 0 to 2𝑛−1, to create an 𝑛× 𝑛S-box. The
implementation of SSEC ensures the reliable extraction of 2𝑛dis-
tinct values for the generation of a valid S-box.

Generation of Resultant S-Box
In this phase to generate a resultant S-box, we use the muta-
tion operation to swap the elements of 𝑆, which we obtained in
Section 3.2, to create a cryptographically strong S-box. The muta-
tion strategy used in our S-box generation method is inspired by
evolutionary operations that introduce structural variation while
maintaining cryptographic constraints. The process operates on
an initial S-box, denoted 𝑆, derived from elliptic curve-based
mapping, and generates mutated versions 𝑆′ through controlled
permutations. This mutation strategy ensures the generation of
structurally diverse S-boxes while preserving bijectivity. By tun-
ing the parameters 𝑘0, 𝑟, and 𝓁, the user can control the trade-off
between similarity to the initial structure and randomness.
The process begins with an initialization step in which we define
an S-box 𝑆of size 𝑛× 𝑛, containing 2𝑛unique elements (typically
𝑛= 8, so |𝑆| = 256). We select an initial index 𝑘0 ∈{0, 1, . . . , 2𝑛−
1}, which serves as the starting point for the mutation trajectory.
The first operation consists of swapping the elements at positions
0 and 𝑘0 in 𝑆, formally:
𝑆[0] ↔𝑆[𝑘0].
Next, we define a fixed mutation step size 𝑟∈ℤ2𝑛, and proceed
with an iterative update process for a total of 𝓁iterations. For each

Security Analysis and Comparison
We analyzed the efficiency of our S-box generation method by
evaluating its dynamic behavior, cryptographic properties, and
computation time. Furthermore, we compared our method with
state-of-the-art approaches. The experiments were conducted on
a Haier Y11c laptop equipped with a 1TB HDD, 8GB RAM, and a
7th-generation Intel Core m3 processor, with speeds ranging from
1.00 to 1.61 GHz, running Windows 10. The software tools used
included Anaconda (Jupyter Notebook) version 3.9 and PyCharm
version 2022.

conducted a comparison between our S-box generator and the

do not exhibit singularities. However, the generators [14, 15, 28]
have singularities. This demonstrates that EC-MutGen is better
than the generators [14, 15, 28], as EC-MutGen can produce
S-boxes without encountering such issues.

initial S-box 𝑆and modified through a sequence of swaps. The
process of Algorithm 2 involves selecting an initial index 𝑘0, a
step size 𝑟, and a number of iterations 𝓁. These parameters intro-
duce variability in the positions where swaps occur, affecting the
final output. The iterative nature of the algorithm, combined with
the specific pattern used for index calculations, ensures the gen-

sequence of swapping indices 𝑘𝑖contribute to a wide range of
permutations. By varying 𝑘0, 𝑟, and 𝓁, the algorithm reduces the
probability of producing identical S-boxes across different runs.

Sensitivity Analysis
In the context of S-boxes, sensitivity refers to the capability of
an S-box generator to produce significantly distinct S-boxes in
response to minor variations in the input parameters [27]. When
an S-box generator demonstrates high sensitivity corresponding
to its input parameters, it is considered resilient against sensi-
tivity and differential attacks. We conducted an analysis of 10 K
S-boxes, determining their minimum, maximum, and average
sensitivity, which produced values of 16, 254, and 246, respec-
tively. Our S-box generator exhibits an average sensitivity of 246,
closely approaching the ideal value of 255. This highlights the fact
that EC-MutGen is highly sensitive.

Analysis of Cryptographic Properties
For analysis of cryptographic properties, we use well-known tests,
namely nonlinearity, algebraic complexity, linear approximation
probability, differential approximation probability, a bit indepen-
dence criterion, and strict avalanche criterion. We evaluate and
compare the cryptographic properties of S-boxes produced using
EC-MutGen and state-of-the-art generators. The comparison is
performed in two different ways: One by generating a sample
of 10 K S-boxes, and the second is performed with the optimal
S-boxes produced by the corresponding generator.
4.2.1
|
Nonlinearity
Nonlinearity (NL) [30] is used to assess how well an S-box is able
to create confusion in a cryptosystem. We have computed the NL
of 10 K S-boxes produced by our generator, and the frequency dis-
tribution of the NL of these 10 K S-boxes is shown in Figure 3. The
results in Figure 3 shows that 93.57% of the 10 K S-boxes produced
by our generator have a NL of 96, indicating that the generator
is capable of producing S-boxes with good resistance to linear
attacks. Moreover, we compared the NL of S-boxes produced by
our generator with those from state-of-the-art generators listed
in Table 7. The results, as shown in Table 7, reveal that our pro-
duced S-boxes show better NL than the S-boxes produced by the
generators [11, 14, 18, 31–43].
4.2.2
|
Algebraic Complexity
The algebraic complexity (AC) of an S-box is determined by
the number of non-zero terms within its associated linear
polynomial [46]. In our analysis, we examined a sample of 10 K
S-boxes produced by EC-MutGen, and the AC values are illus-
trated in Figure 4. It is evident from Figure 4 that AC values fall
within the range [249, 255], and in numerous instances, the AC
value is equal to the optimal value of 255.
Furthermore, we conducted a comparison of the AC values for
our generated S-boxes with those produced by state-of-the-art
generators listed in Table 7. The results, as shown in Table 7, indi-
cate that the AC of our S-boxes is better than those produced by
generators [9, 15, 17, 33, 36–41, 45].
4.2.3
|
Linear Approximation Probability
The linear approximation probability (LAP) quantifies the resis-
tance of an S-box to linear attacks [47]. The quality of an S-box
depends on its ability to withstand linear attacks. A low LAP
value indicates a high level of resistance against such attacks.
We have performed LAP computations for a total of 10 K
S-boxes produced by our generator. The maximum LAP value
of these 10 K S-boxes is presented in Figure 5. The results
show that the LAP values for this set of 10 K S-boxes fall
within the range of [0.125, 0.164], which is close to the optimal
value of 0.
Additionally, we have conducted a comparison of the maximum
LAP values of our S-boxes with those produced by state-of-the-art
methods. in Table 7, it becomes evident that our generated
S-boxes exhibit the superior LAP values in comparison to those
presented in [1, 10, 14, 16–18, 27, 32, 36, 38, 39, 44]. Conse-
quently, it can be concluded that our S-boxes offer robust resis-
tance against linear attacks.

Phase-1: Generation of Diffusion in the
Plain-Image
In this phase, we use a linear congruential generator (LCG) [53] to
generate a sequence of pseudo-random numbers of length 𝑢× 𝑣.
This sequence is used to enhance the diffusion of pixel values in
𝐼𝑃. The LCG is defined by the recurrence relation:
𝑟𝓁+1 = (𝛼× 𝑟𝓁+ 𝛽) mod 𝑚,
(1)
where 𝑟0 is the initial value, 𝛼is the multiplier, 𝛽is the increment,
𝑚is the modulus, and 0 ≤𝓁≤(𝑢× 𝑣). The following conditions
are imposed to ensure desirable statistical properties of the gen-
erated sequence: 𝑚> 0, 0 < 𝛼< 𝑚, 0 ≤𝛽< 𝑚, and 0 ≤𝑟0 < 𝑚.
Furthermore, to achieve a full-period LCG, gcd(𝛽, 𝑚) = 1. In our
scheme, the LCG-generated pseudo-random sequence is used to
control the substitution phase. During this phase, the generated
values are XORed with pixel intensities to enhance diffusion. The
effectiveness and unpredictability of the encryption process are
closely tied to the statistical quality of the LCG output.
Let 𝑅= {𝑟1, 𝑟2, . . . , 𝑟𝑢×𝑣} denote the sequence of pseudo-random
numbers generated by the LCG. To introduce diffusion in 𝐼𝑃, a
bitwise XOR operation is performed between 𝐼𝑃and the random
sequence 𝑅. This results in a diffused image 𝐼Diffused:
𝐼𝐷= 𝐼𝑃⊕𝑅,
(2)
where ⊕represents the XOR operation. This step introduces ran-
domness into the plain image by applying the LCG-generated
random numbers to diffuse the pixel values, thus enhancing the
security through diffusion.
5.2
|
Phase-2: Generation of Confusion in the
Diffused Image
The second phase focuses on creating confusion within 𝐼Diffused,
thus minimizing the correlation between adjacent pixels. Confu-
sion is crucial in an encryption scheme because high correlation
among adjacent pixels is a well-known vulnerability that can be
exploited in cryptanalysis attacks. In this phase, we use our gener-
ated S-boxes to scramble the pixel values, ensuring that adjacent
pixels in the encrypted image are unrelated. Let 𝜎𝑢and 𝜎𝑣be two
S-boxes generated using our S-box generator. The confusion pro-
cess involves the following steps:
i. Column Permutation: The diffused image 𝐼Diffused goes
through a column permutation using S-box 𝜎𝑣. This oper-
ation shuffles the columns of 𝐼Diffused based on the order
specified by 𝜎𝑣, resulting in 𝐼′
Confused.
ii. Row Permutation: After column permutation, the rows of
𝐼′
Confused are permuted using S-box 𝜎𝑢. This step results in
the confused image 𝐼Confused, ensuring that both columns
and rows of the image are scrambled. This shuffling of the
pixels within each row and within each column of 𝐼Confused
using 𝜎𝑣and 𝜎𝑢leads to the final encrypted image 𝐼Encrypted.
By performing these operations, we enhance the confusion in
the image, ensuring that the final encrypted image exhibits no
observable patterns or correlations that could be exploited in
cryptanalysis.

Abstract: Efficient generation of substitution boxes (S-boxes) with strong cryptographic properties is essential for securing modern digital systems, particularly in resource-constrained environments such as the Internet of Things (IoT) and cloud computing. However, constructing dynamic S-boxes often incurs significant computational overhead, which can affect encryption performance. We propose an efficient S-box generation algorithm that combines elliptic curve point generation with a mutation-based optimization. Our approach constructs cryptographically robust 𝑛× 𝑛S-boxes in three stages: (1) generating points on an elliptic curve over a finite field, (2) generating an initial S-box from these points, and (3) applying a mutation operation to improve nonlinearity and other cryptographic properties. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that the proposed method generates a secure 8 × 8 S-box on an average of 0.0009 s and produces 10,000 randomized S-boxes in 1.2169 s. Comparative analysis indicates that our generator operates at a speed of at least eight times faster than existing state-of-the-art generators, without compromising security against standard cryptanalytic attacks. We further validate the practical utility of our generator in the context of image encryption. The results show that the method effectively secures the image data, even when the original image exhibits high inter-pixel correlation, highlighting its applicability to real-world cryptographic systems.
